headline: Trump reinstates a naval blockade on Iranian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — oil jumps to four-week highs and KSE-100 skids another ~2% intraday on top of Monday's rout, with autos, cement, banks, E&P and OMCs all bleeding together.
summary: The story hasn't changed direction today, it's just gotten louder. The US announced it is reinstating a naval blockade of Iranian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz effective today, plus a 20% fee on cargo transiting the strait, and Brent/WTI both pushed to four-week highs (Brent $84.73, +1.7% on the day; WTI $79.62, +1.9%) — VIX is up 14% too, a classic risk-off signature. KSE-100 opened straight into the selling, falling from Monday's close of 179,927 to an intraday band of roughly 176,200-176,460 (down ~2%), on top of yesterday's 1.27% drop and its ugly 13-up/87-down breadth. Pakistan's own government has already warned this exact scenario — a blocked Hormuz transit route that carries over 80% of the country's crude imports, plus GCC remittance exposure — could triple the weekly oil import bill and push CPI back toward 15-17%; the fuel-price pass-through is already live (petrol/diesel hiked mid-month, now reviewed weekly instead of fortnightly). The regime call stays risk-off: the desk is leaning defensive, watching quality names with real earnings and dividend cover rather than chasing anything into this tape.

sectors.name: Banks
sectors.why: Macro still tags banks favoured on rate-carry (SBP policy rate 11.5%) and dividend cover, but UBL, MCB, MEBL, NBP and HBL all traded red again today per the wire — no rush to add into a broad selloff.

sectors.name: E&P
sectors.why: Higher crude (Brent $84.73, +1.7% today) should lift realized oil/gas prices for OGDC, PPL and MARI, but all three sold off again today with the broader market — the fundamental tailwind hasn't shown up in the price yet.

sectors.name: OMCs
sectors.why: PSO faces weekly-repriced fuel costs and circular-debt risk when crude spikes this fast, and its own net margin is a wafer-thin 1.4% — almost no cushion if costs move faster than pricing approvals.

sectors.name: Autos
sectors.why: Imported-input costs and a weaker consumer under rising fuel prices squeeze the sector; HCAR and INDU were both down over the prior 5 sessions (-5.3% and -4.0%) even before today's blockade headline.

sectors.name: Cement
sectors.why: Cement runs on imported coal and fuel, and it showed: DGKC, MLCF and FCCL each fell more than 3% at Monday's close alone, before today's fresh oil spike.

sectors.name: Refineries
sectors.why: ATRL, NRL and PRL were the lone gainers Monday on a new $6bn refinery-upgrade policy plus firmer product cracks from pricier crude, but thin net margins (NRL ~2%, ATRL ~7%) mean that tailwind could reverse fast if crude keeps climbing.

watchlist.angle: The desk's golden-cross trigger (SMA50>SMA200) fired on HCAR today — on its own 10-trade history that setup has won 60% of the time for +3.1% net per trade, still profitable out-of-sample (confidence: high, per live_triggers.json). But it's an auto stock firing straight into the sector this Hormuz shock is hitting hardest, and its fundamental read is 'caution' (P/E 10.65 in the priciest third, thin 2.6% net margin) — the technical signal and today's news are pulling in opposite directions.
watchlist.risk: Autos carry direct imported-input-cost and demand exposure to a sustained oil/PKR shock, which is exactly the 'avoid' sector macro.json flags for this regime; a confirmed (not just threatened) Hormuz closure would hit this thesis hardest of anything on the list.

watchlist.angle: The second live trigger on the board: GAL's 'trend + momentum combo' fired today too (57% historical hit rate over 37 trades, +1.3% net/trade, confidence: medium). Fundamentals are only 'mixed' — cheap P/E (5.17) and an improving forward multiple, but small-cap (Rs34.6bn market cap) with a small dividend. Same sector conflict as HCAR: the signal is real, but it's firing into autos while autos are under direct pressure.
watchlist.risk: Small-cap, thinner-liquidity name in a sector the desk currently avoids on macro grounds — a further oil or PKR leg would squeeze margins and consumer demand at the same time.

watchlist.angle: No live trigger has fired yet, but UBL sits on the strongest proven technical edge anywhere on the strategy map right now: its 'consolidation break' setup has won 76% of 38 historical trades for +2.2% net each, holding up at 80% out-of-sample. Fundamentals back it up — an 'attractive' rating, P/E 8.38, and a 6.72% dividend covered at just a 50% payout — and results land 2026-07-22, about a week out.
watchlist.risk: UBL still fell 1.6% today alongside every other bank on the oil-shock tape; a hawkish surprise at the July 27 SBP meeting (if this fuel shock reignites CPI) would remove the rate-carry cushion that makes banks attractive right now.

watchlist.angle: OGDC is the textbook beneficiary of exactly what's moving markets today — a higher realized oil and gas price. The desk's own valuation composite has it undervalued by roughly 33% against fair value, profitability is strong (40% net margin), and its '52-week high breakout' strategy carries a 63% historical hit rate. No trigger has fired yet, so this is one to watch, not chase.
watchlist.risk: The fundamental tailwind hasn't shown up in the price — OGDC fell again today with the rest of the market, a reminder that in a risk-off panic even direct beneficiaries get sold first and questions get asked later.

watchlist.angle: MCB screens 'attractive': a covered 8.63% dividend (74% payout), an improving forward P/E (7.7 vs 8.59 trailing), and a proven Bollinger-squeeze-breakout edge (62% hit rate historically). Results are due 2026-08-07 — no live trigger yet, but a name the desk is content to watch through the volatility given the 11.5% policy rate still feeds bank earnings.
watchlist.risk: Like every bank today, MCB traded lower on the broad selloff; sustained PKR weakness or a CPI re-acceleration from this fuel shock could pressure the rate-carry story before results land.

catalysts.event: SBP MPC — first monetary policy decision of FY27; watch for a hawkish tilt if this fuel-price shock feeds into CPI
PBS July 2026 CPI release — first print to capture the mid-July fuel hikes and any further weekly adjustments
MEBL, LUCK, MCB, MARI and FCCL quarterly results

risks: A confirmed, sustained Strait of Hormuz closure (beyond today's blockade-and-fee action) would be a much bigger shock than what's priced in — Pakistan's own Ministry of Economic Affairs warned in April 2026 that this exact scenario already tripled the weekly oil import bill from roughly $300mn to $800mn, and PIDE has flagged CPI could re-accelerate to 15-17% YoY under a severe, sustained disruption.

SBP's July 27 MPC (first FY27 decision) is the near-term swing factor — CPI eased to 11.1% in June, but the mid-month fuel hike and the new weekly pricing-review regime mean a hawkish hold or surprise tightening is live if this shock persists.

GCC states supply 55% of Pakistan's remittances (about 4.7% of GDP); a prolonged Gulf slowdown tied to this conflict would hit that inflow channel just as the oil import bill is rising — a pincer on the external account that the current-account surplus buffer wasn't built to absorb.
